title: 'Why Are Kashmiri Actors Always Terrorists?': Bollywood's Typecasting Debate
excerpt: Filmmakers and critics say Hindi cinema keeps casting Kashmiri performers in one role — the militant — and rarely lets them play anything else.
body:
• Filmmakers and critics are calling out Bollywood for reducing Kashmiri actors to a single screen identity: the terrorist.
  • Actor Aparshakti Khurana, who played a Kashmiri terrorist in 2022's Dhokha Round D Corner, learned the Kashmiri language for the role — while broader, non-militant roles continue to elude Kashmiri performers.
  • Documentary filmmaker Sanjay Kak told the BBC: "It's not been told by Bollywood but Bollywood doesn't tell these stories."
  • Critics trace the pattern from Roja and Mission Kashmir to The Kashmir Files, arguing the industry has cemented a "Kashmir equals terrorism" equation on screen.

"Why are Kashmiri actors always terrorists?" The question, posed by filmmakers confronting Bollywood's casting habits, has sharpened into one of the industry's most uncomfortable debates: why does Hindi cinema keep handing Kashmiri performers the same role — the militant, the separatist, the man with the gun?

The pattern is familiar to anyone who watches Bollywood. When the plot needs a terrorist, the casting shorthand is predictable: a Kashmiri Muslim character, often the only Kashmiri in the film, radicalised, bearded, and doomed. Critics argue it has become a reflex — and Kashmiri actors say it has become a trap.

The formula on screen

Writer Kaif Ansari, in a widely shared analysis of Bollywood's "terrorist Muslim" trope, laid out the blueprint the industry has followed for three decades: "Need a villain? Make him Muslim. Need a terrorist? Add a beard, kajal, topi, Arabic words, and boom — the 'threat' is ready." The films that seeded the stereotype, he argues, include Roja (1992), Sarfarosh (1999), Fiza (2000) and Mission Kashmir (2000) — with Roja and Mission Kashmir, in his words, creating "the image that Kashmir = Muslim terrorism."

Academic research has reached similar conclusions. A peer-reviewed study of Bollywood's portrayal of Kashmir found the industry repeatedly constructing a "threatening Kashmiri identity" in which Muslim Kashmiris appear as terrorists or as Indians committing sedition, while "good" Kashmiris are those absorbed into the dominant cultural mainstream.

Actors caught in the loop

The typecasting is not abstract for the actors living it. Aparshakti Khurana, known for comic roles, took a deliberate departure in 2022 to play a Kashmiri terrorist in Dhokha Round D Corner — and threw himself into the part's authenticity.

"I play a Kashmiri terrorist in the film. I hired and worked extensively to learn Kashmiri language for my character... I have tried to show a different side of myself as a performer."

— Aparshakti Khurana, actor

That even established actors must pass through the militant role to prove their range is, for critics, the point. The industry's demand for Kashmiri authenticity extends to dialect coaches and lean, battle-worn looks — but rarely to Kashmiri protagonists who are teachers, lovers, or simply ordinary people.

What filmmakers are saying

The sharpest criticism comes from filmmakers who have tried to tell Kashmiri stories differently. Sanjay Kak, a Kashmiri Pandit documentary filmmaker who has covered the region extensively, pushed back on the claim that Bollywood had finally told the Kashmiri Pandit story with The Kashmir Files.

"I'm a little baffled by this constant refrain that this is a story that has not been told. It's not been told by Bollywood but Bollywood doesn't tell these stories."

— Sanjay Kak, documentary filmmaker, to the BBC

The Kashmir Files itself became the flashpoint for the debate. Reviewing it for The Indian Express, Shubhra Gupta called it "a work of propaganda aligned with the ruling party's discourse," while The Hindu's Anuj Kumar described it as "historical revisionism, sprinkled with some facts, some half-truths, and plenty of distortions." A court even restrained director Vivek Agnihotri from including scenes depicting an air force squadron leader's death after the officer's wife sued over factual inaccuracies. Analysts noted the film's visual grammar — long beards, Islamic headgear and dark garments marking Muslim characters as cultural outsiders and physical threats.

The road ahead

Those calling for change argue the fix is structural: more Kashmiri writers, directors and producers with the power to greenlight stories, and casting that treats Kashmiris as characters rather than costumes. Streaming platforms have opened some space — but on the big screen, the militant with a Kashmiri accent remains Bollywood's default. For diaspora audiences, who often encounter Kashmir only through these films, the stakes are real: cinema is, for many abroad, the primary image of the Valley they will ever see. Until the industry lets Kashmiri actors play anything else, that image will stay frozen in a single frame.
